title: Nerves on radio and records; Carroll Dickerson and Zutty at the Grand Terrace
summary: He never played his best on air or on record, recalls a bad Richard Jones date, a radio mix-up at the Grand Terrace, and the 1935 Helen Oakley session.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: What was it like to be on the radio?

On the radio? Well, I imagine a fella, speaking personally, a fella's inclined to tighten up on making records on the radio. I know I always do. I've never played my best on any radio or either records. I don't know why. I don't know, it just seemed to get kind of nervous, you know, you want to do your best, and one of those things, you know. And you're not there, you just don't play as, at least I don't, as freely as you like to play, or as you can play. See, because you know a thousand people's going to hear it, maybe me. Now I recorded it with Richard Jones, and it was just a Hopscotch blues. I made it good with Jimmy Newman. I started out, da The Mish Club was one of them. I don't know what was wrong. We had, we made it on another, we made it on another, we recorded again with Jones. And it's something I can never forget. It was pitiful. It seemed like my breathing was bad, you know. And I just, I didn't think there was a good relief. He told me he wasn't released that tune, that record. I begged him not to because I knew I wasn't up to poor. I hadn't been playing for about three months or so, you know. He'd been sick. And he released it anyhow. And I didn't hear the record anymore until I was up to Dr. Valmer's house, of Larchmont in New York. He had this, and he played it. And I was sick, it was terrible. And he wrote it up in the downbeatin'. And he said, this Edmund Hall, you know, they had him in a blindfold. And he said, now these are good musicians. He said, it's a shame. How bad this record sounds. And he wasn't lying. I ruined the record myself, you understand? He wasn't lying.
He should have taken some muscle tone.
Did you ever hear of muscle tone?
Yeah, I heard of it. You know?
Mm-hmm. And that's what Frankie Halfbint used to advertise. Yeah.

On the radio. Well, he had a good chance. We broadcast one night. And I don't know, it's just like I said at Titanes. We rehearsed before then and the man sounded good. But when we got on the air, it sounded all together different. And it seems like some people, Titans up, you know, to get those butterflies in here, you know? And they just don't produce as well as if you was playing for a dance or a live. Loose. Just like playing music note for note and playing without the music. Yeah. Well, you just can relax, you know, and play. Yeah. Well, therefore, well, if you have a leader in front of you, and you have these arrangements, you're part of a section and all that stuff, you're on there. Now, I was with Carol Dixon at the Grand Terrace, and this is when a fellow needs a friend. I don't know, they flew around and the Reeds had one tune and the Brass had another one. So we were on the air. So when it started off, they playing one tune and we playing another one. And it taken us about, well about a minute. You know, a minute is a long time, the keys like that, before we could adjust everything. But the damage had been done. And then a lot of times, Zooty and Carol Dixon were pretty good friends, but they'd get into it. Maybe it'd be right on there. And Zooty said, oh go to hell, God damn. Come on, Zooty, come on, Zooty, come on, Zooty. And you'd think they were going to fight, but that morning, 55th Street was the main drag then. They'd gone out to 55th Street. And so a relative of Carol's wife gave me a picture of the band, not this particular band, a little later on. And they're supposed to give me some more material, you know. But Carol was a good leader, a good fiddle player. But Zooty, Zooty was something else. Then we made some recordings for the English girl, Helen Oakley. We had Jabril Smith, yeah we have him, Jabril Smith. We had Jabril Smith, myself, and the two Marcella brothers, Marty and I forget the others.

Yeah, Joe. And then we had this guy, Charles Levere. And we had Zooty, and then we had Bill and Huey Long, Huey Long guitar player, Bill was a bass player. He committed suicide, so to say, about a year or so ago. Some people say he didn't, some say he's a nice bass player. Anyhow, we did the recording. And I heard him recently, and it did sound bad. But I understand she's living in New York State now. But we never did receive any money from that. Never did.
That would have been a good time to get some money. Yeah. 1935. Yeah.
